TARGETED TEMPERATURE MANAGEMENT AFTER CARDIAC ARREST




Rationale: Fever is associated with worse neurological outcomes and neuronal damage due to inflammatory changes and biochemical cascades that develop following ischemia and reperfusion injury associated with cardiac arrest (Arch Intern Med 2001). TTM is a class I recommendation for all patients not following commands post arrest (AHA 2023). Goal is to avoid fever for neuroprotection and to be




aggressive about diagnosing/treating infections.




Causes of fever: Inflammatory response to global ischemia-reperfusion, drug fever, and/or infection




• High infection risk in all post arrest patients from aspiration/pneumonia, global ischemia -> gut ischemia -> bacterial translocation. Pan-culture and consider empiric antibiotic treatment.




• If on temperature control device preventing rise in temperature, potential fevers will present as changes in cooling pattern




*




TTM options if patient is not following commands (patient needs to be stable enough to wean sedation and paralysis for this exam):




• Normothermia (≤37.5 C)




◦ Allow passive rewarming until patient achieves T 37 C. Once at 37 C, use temp control device




◦ Arctic Sun or other temperature control device to maintain T <37.5 C for 72 hr




• Mild Hypothermia (T 33-36 C)




◦ Individualized patient selection for mild hypothermia (T 33-36 C) decided by primary team and Neurology




◦ Temperature control device placed as soon as possible with goal of achieving target temp within 4h of ROSC




◦ Maintain mild hypothermia for 24 hr, followed by normothermia for 48hr for total 72 hr




◦ For mild hypothermia, re-warming should occur at a target rate of 0.25 °C/h until normothermia achieved.




◦ Monitor blood glucose/electrolytes closely




o Relative Contraindications to Mild Hypothermia: Refractory hypotension, Recent head trauma, active bleeding, major surgery (<14d)




Evidence:




- Targeted hypothermia (T 33 C) did not reduce 6-month mortality or survival with good neurologic outcome compared to targeted normothermia (T<37.5 C) (NEJM 2021;384:2283)




- Whether certain subgroups benefit from targeted hypothermia is uncertain (e.g., initial non-shockable rhythm (NEJM 2019;381:2327))




- Currently insufficient evidence to recommend different therapeutic temperatures for specific cardiac arrest groups (Class 2b, AHA 2023)




Sedation and Analgesia:




- Patients should undergo continuous sedation/analgesia if undergoing TTM w/mild hypothermia. Propofol is preferred sedative agent, dilaudid (or fentanyl) is preferred analgesic




Shivering:




- Stepwise approach to shivering in pts undergoing TTM (1st line: PR/PO acetaminophen 650q6 → IV, Mg >3, 2nd line: skin counterwarming + dexmedetomidine OR propofol OR hydromorphone boluses, 3rd line: propofol + hydromorphone gtt, consider buspirone 30q8, 4th line: NMBA) (Neurocrit Care 2011;14:389)




Neuro-prognostication see Neurology section

topics.text:
Management

Bradycardia with Pulse 




HR<60 bpm and symptomatic 




 Circ 2020 Evidence Review | ACC/AHA Brady 2018  








ASSESS PATIENT 




• Focused exam → vitals, mental status, pupils,  pulmonary edema, murmurs, warm/cold 




• Review recent ECG, tele/labs, meds/dose changes  




• Obtain 12-Lead ECG, have pacing pads available,  call for atropine to bedside (may take time)  




• IV Access: BMP, Mg, lactate ± trop 




• Monitor BP freq., keep O2 > 92%, maintain airway     








PATIENT UNSTABLE IF: 




 Any of the following present 




◦ Hypotension/shock 




◦ Altered mental status 




◦ Ischemic chest discomfort 




◦ Acute heart failure/pulmonary edema 








             Trial medications 




Low threshold to jump to pacing 




ATROPINE 




1mg bolus | q3-5mins (max 3mg); 2hr half-life 




do not give s/p heart transplant 




  avoid with AV block Mobitz II or CHB    




& ANTIDOTES BY CAUSE 




DOPAMINE IV infusion   5-20mcg/kg/min 




OR 




EPINEPHRINE IV infusion   2-10mcg/min 








Transcutaneous vs venous pacing 




TRANSCUTANEOUS PACING  




- Basics: Emergent 2mg lorazepam + 2mg dilaudid      → turn to PACER → SET RATE: 100   BPM + SET OUTPUT: 100 mA → turn output down to minimum needed   to capture → adjust rate down based on hemodynamics  




TRANSVENOUS PACING WIRE  




- Wire placed by cardiology  




- Indications: 1) need for transcutaneous pacing despite meds, 2)   unstable rhythm with no quickly reversible cause  








IF PATIENT IS STABLE:  




Monitor + Assess for reversible causes 




- Mobitz II & CHB with wide QRS → often gets pacing wire even if   stable, call cards + ensure prepared to pace  




- HOLD nodal blockers/anti-HTN if applicable  












Bradycardia diagnostic algorithm

Bradycardia Diagnostic Algorithm 




Bold = call Cards   to consider pacing

Yes

2. Mobitz I w/ 2:1 block 




3. Mobitz II (# of P > #  of QRS)

2. CHB w/ junctional escape  OR ventricular escape if wide  QRS (Ps unrelated to QRS)

2. Wandering pacemaker 




3. Non-conducting  PACs 













No 




1. Sinus arrest w/ junctional  escape OR ventricular escape  [idioventricular]* 




2. A fib/flutter w/ slow/variable  conduction 

















Rhythm pearls

RHYTHM PEARLS 




- If grouped beats → look for Mobitz I & II  




- In 2nd degree AV block with 2:1 conduction, it is not possible to  differentiate Mobitz I vs. Mobitz II  




- Always remember to consider hyperkalemia!  







Etiologies



ETIOLOGIES OF SINUS BRADYCARDIA  AND/OR CHB  




Primarily SB 




Primarily CHB 




-SSS




-Elevated ICP




-Hypothermia




-Hypothyroidism




-Hypoxia




-Sleep apnea




-Carotid dz + recent stent




-s/p TAVR




-s/p septal ablation




-Endocarditis




Both 




-Ischemia/ACS (inferior MI  commonly)




-Increased vagal tone




-Meds/toxins (esp in  liver/renal disease)




-Hyperkalemia




-Degenerative, calcific  conduction dz




-Infiltrative disease




-Lyme myocarditis




-Autoimmune myocarditis




-Pericarditis





Specific antidotes by cause

SPECIFIC ANTIDOTES BY CAUSE 




- Beta blocker: glucagon 3-10mg IV (if no response, repeat  bolus, if response, infusion at 3-5mg/h) 




- Calcium channel blocker: glucagon as above, calcium  gluconate 3-6g q10-20min or gtt, insulin 1U/kg bolus with  0.5U/kg gtt 




- Digoxin: dig immune FAB vial, 1 vial binds ~ 0.5mg  digoxin, administer over 30min 




- Opioids: naloxone 0.4-0.8mg IV, consider gtt 




- Organophosphate: atropine 2-5mg IV (double dose  q5min until effect), pralidoxime 1-2g IV over 15-30min 







Atropine & AV blocks

ATROPINE & AV BLOCKS  




Take-home message: Atropine will not help in the setting of CHB and   Mobitz II  




◦ Ineffective for blocks below AV node (↓response to atropine in pt with   AVB; Resuscitation 1999;41:47)   




◦ Potential worsening of Mobitz II 2/2 ↑HR (Am J Card 1974;33:333)

Assessment

  Tachycardia with Pulse  




HR>120 bpm and symptomatic 




ACLS Guidelines 2020 








 ASSESS PATIENT 




• Focused exam → vitals, MS, pulmonary edema,  murmurs, warm/cold, pupils, other sx 




• Review: most recent ECG, tele, labs, meds, events  




 • Obtain: 12-Lead ECG, Defib + pads

 ◦ Correct all electrolyte abnormalities 




• Monitor BP frequently 




• O2: supplement to >92%, maintain airway 








IS THE PATIENT UNSTABLE?

 Lido generally safe →  effective for all PMVT and will   not worsen pre-excited rhythms 












Acute drug dosing

ACUTE DRUG DOSING  




• Adenosine: 6mg rapid IV push (followed by NS flush) + arm raise, can  repeat x1 → 12mg if required, central line = ½ peripheral dose, relative  contraindication in pts s/p heart transplant 




• Amiodarone: 150mg IV over 10min (may repeat x1); then infusion at  1mg/min x6h followed by 0.5mg/min x18h (max 2.2g/24h) 




• Diltiazem: 0.25mg/kg IV bolus over 2min → gtt (avoid if LVEF unknown) 




• Lidocaine: 1.0-1.5mg/kg IV bolus (usually 100mg), refractory → repeat  0.5-0.75mg/kg IV push q5-10min PRN, max 3mg/kg → maintenance  infusion at 1-4mg/min; preferred agent if ↑QTc 




• Metoprolol: IV push 2.5-5 mg over 2 min; repeat q5 min; max dose  15mg; start low and increase; follow with oral after IV rate control 




• Procainamide: 20-50mg/min or 100mg q5min until any of the following:  arrhythmia terminates, ↓BP, QRS prolongs by 50% from baseline, or total  17mg/kg given → maintenance infusion at 1-4mg/min (adjusted for CrCl),  avoid with ↑QTc 




• Sotalol: 1-1.5mg/kg IV over 5 min; then maintenance infusion at  10mg/min, contraindicated with ↑QTc & caution in pts w/ ↓EF 







Vagal maneuvers

VAGAL MANEUVERS:   




- Unilateral Carotid Massage: supine with neck extended → steady pressure to carotid sinus (inferior to angle of the mandible at level of  thyroid cartilage near carotid pulse), avoid if prior TIA/CVA in past 3mo, and those with carotid bruits; 5%-33% success 




- Modified Valsalva Maneuver: semi-recumbent → blow forcefully into a 10cc syringe x10-15 seconds → reposition to supine and  passively raise legs at 45° for 15 seconds; 43% effective in breaking SVTs vs 17% with standard Valsalva (Lancet 2015;386:1747) 




- Also consider: cold ice face immersion or ice-water bag to face (diving reflex, more effective in children); 17% success.

topics.text:
EXTERNAL DEFIBRILLATION/CARDIOVERSION/TRANSCUTANEOUS PACING
• About the device: . This device allows for external defibrillation, cardioversion, and pacing with additional benefits (e.g. display ET-CO2, CPR quality feedback, & upload rhythm strips into Epic)




• Additional supplies/resources: Ambu bag, intubation equipment, , backboard, suction, LUCAS (cardiopulm assist system)




Medications: use procedural sedation (typically 50mcg fentanyl → 2mg midazolam) when possible, . In emergent situations, Dilaudid 1-2mg + lorazepam 2mg is a reasonable alternative (often readily available).




DISPLAY/OPERATION OF ZOLL R SERIES
• Remove all clothing covering the patient’s chest. Dry chest if necessary. If the patient has excessive chest hair, shave it to ensure proper adhesion of the electrodes. Can rip off hair with extra set of pads if razor not readily available in acute situations.




• Attach hands-free therapy electrodes in anteroapical position (pictured) or anteroposterior position for defibrillation. Some evidence that pads should be placed in anteroposterior position for pacing if possible (AHA 2022, Resuscitation 2022)








Pearls:




• CPR ok to perform while pacing, take R- sided pulses (L not reliable)




• Failure to capture? Increase output, ensure pads are in correct location (avoid bony structures), consider ddx (barrel chest, COPD, hypoxia, tamponade/pericardial effusion, pneumothorax, acidosis, hyperK, obesity, MI, cardiac drug tox [dig, anti-arrhythmic])




• Failure to sense? Only happens with synchronous pacing – can switch to asynchronous pacing, reposition pads





















FIRST turn the Selector Switch to ON. Then press Manual (bottom left soft key) to change to ALS




Defibrillation




Synchronized Cardioversion




Transcutaneous Pacing




Indications: Pulseless VT or VF




Indications: Unstable SVT or VT




Indications: Unstable bradycardia




1. Default energy selection is 120 J.




Initial dose 120-200 J. Use Energy Select (UP) & (DOWN) arrow keys to change the energy.




2. If there is a shockable rhythm on the pulse/rhythm check, press Charge. Continue CPR while charging.




3. Once charged, the red shock




button illuminates. Shout “Clear!”




then press and hold the illuminated Shock button at the top right of the console.




4. Resume CPR for 2 minutes before the next pulse/rhythm check




1. Select the desired energy using the up and down arrow keys on the front panel




• Narrow, regular: 50-100 J (atrial flutter often converts with 50 J)




• Narrow, irregular: 120-200 J (atrial fibrillation typically requires 150 J)




• Wide, regular: 100 J




• Wide, irregular: 150-200 J (defib dose)




2. Press the Sync On/Off button




• Confirm that a Sync marker (⬇) appears on the monitor above each detected R- wave to indicate where discharge will occur




• If necessary, use the LEAD and SIZE buttons to establish settings that yield the best display




3. Press the CHARGE button on the front panel. Ensure patient is “clear”




4. Press and hold the illuminated SHOCK button on the front panel. The defibrillator will discharge with the next detected R wave




5. If additional shocks are necessary, increase the energy level as needed




• Confirm that a Sync marker (⬇) appears above each R-wave; you may need to press Sync between shocks




6. Anticoagulation required for at least four weeks after cardioversion




1. PACER appears as an option on the




Selector Switch. Turn to PACER




2. Set the PACER RATE (BPM) to a value




20 bpm higher than the patient’s intrinsic heart rate. If unknown or absent intrinsic rate, use 100 bpm




• Observe the pacing stimulus marker on the display and verify that it is well-positioned in diastole




3. Increase PACER OUTPUT (mA) until the paced beats demonstrate capture (“threshold”); the output value is displayed on the screen.




• Capture = widened QRS complex + loss of underlying intrinsic rhythm




• Confirm mechanical capture with pulse check and/or by observing ventricular contraction w/ US




4. Set the PACER OUTPUT to the lowest setting that maintains consistent capture




• Usually ~10% above threshold (typical threshold: ~40-80 mA)




• Pressing and holding the 4:1 button temporarily withholds pacing stimuli, thereby allowing you to observe pt’s underlying EKG rhythm & morphology




• Treat underlying cause and/or pursue transvenous/permanent pacing

• Clockwise/counterclockwise rotation (“R wave progression”): R wave amplitude typically increases from V1 to V5, amplitude of R becomes greater than S at V3 or V4. Early or late R wave progression is nonspecific and can be normal (AmHeartJ2004;148:80)




◦ CCW (“early R wave progression”): R>S prior to V3. Causes: RVH, WPW, LAFB, posterior MI.




◦ CW (“late R wave progression”): R>S after V4. Causes: cardiomyopathy, LVH, LBBB, anterior MI.




• Low voltage: average QRS amplitude <5 mm in I, II, III and <10 mm in precordial leads




◦ DDx: obesity, pericardial effusion, PTX, COPD, PE, restrictive or infiltrative CM (particularly amyloidosis), severe hypothyroidism, or anasarca




COMPLEXES AND INTERVALS (Circ 2009;119:e241)
• P wave: right and left atrial depolarization. Normal: duration <120ms, voltage ≥ 0.1mV in I, area (1/2 duration x voltage in II) ≤ 4 (Circ Arrhythm Electrophysiol. 2022; e010435)




• PR interval: atrial depolarization, AV node and His-Purkinje conduction. Normally 140-200ms, changes with rate (shortened at faster rates, longer at lower rates) d/t autonomic effects on AV nodal conduction




• QRS: ventricular depolarization. Normal duration 60-110ms, not influenced by HR. QRS 100-120ms = incomplete BBB or intraventricular conduction delay (IVCD). QRS >120ms = BBB, ventricular activation (PVC, VT, fusion beats, WPW, paced beats), hyperK, Na channel poisoning, aberrancy,






hypothermia.






LAFB: left axis deviation, QRS <120 unless RBBB, qR in I, aVL and rS in II, III, aVF. Common, nonspecific.









LPFB: right axis deviation, QRS <120 unless RBBB, rS in I, aVL and qR in II, III, aVF. Rare in isolation, usually w/ RBBB.











• ST segment: normally isoelectic plateau of ventricular potentials







RBBB: QRS >120, rSR’ in V1 or V2, wide qRS in V6, S>R duration in I, V6. Causes: infection (myocarditis), infarction, increased RV pressure (PE,




Bifascicular: RBBB + LAFB or LPFB









LBBB: QRS >120, wide negative QS in V1, wide tall R in I, aVL, V5, V6. Causes: primarily dilated cardiomyopathy (ischemia, infection, valv












• T wave: ventricular repolarization, with a slow upstroke and a rapid return to the isoelectric line after peaking. Usually asymmetric and in the same direction as the QRS. Should have smooth contours (bumps in T are usually buried P waves)




• U wave: If present, will be right after and in same direction as T wave, shorter at faster rates; DDx: bradycardia, hypoK/Mg/Ca, hypothermia




• QT interval: ventricular depolarization and repolarization. Excludes U wave unless fused with T wave. Rate-dependent (shortened at faster rates). Normal <440ms (M) and <460ms (F). Reassuring if QT is less than half R-R interval with normal HR

rare: ventricular depolarization through bypass tract instead causing wide complex tachycardia

Either from multiple atrial pacemaker sites or single focus with different conduction properties

topics.text:
WIDE COMPLEX TACHYCARDIA (QRS ≥120MS)
DDx = VT (80%), SVT with aberrant conduction, pre-excitation syndrome, or pacemaker-mediated tachycardia







Features that Favor VT (note: absence does NOT rule out VT)




Features that Favor SVT with Aberrancy




• History of structural heart disease, prior MI, ICD




• Very wide QRS (>160 ms), Rate > 120 (if <120, consider Na channel toxicity or VT in someone already on significant antiarrhythmics)




• New northwest (aka extreme) axis (leads I and II negative)




• AV dissociation (often V rate > A rate): pathognomonic for VT




• Concordance: all QRS in V1-6 are completely (+) or completely (-)




• Partial (fusion beat) or complete (capture beat) depolarization of His- Purkinje by a competing supraventricular (atrial / junctional) rhythm




• Basel algorithm = VT likely if ≥2 of 3 present: (1) high risk substrate (prior MI, EF<35, prior VT/has ICD), (2) lead II time to first peak >40ms (1 small box), (3) aVR time to first peak >40ms (1 small box).




▪ Very effective: 93% sensitive & 90% specific (JACC 2022;7:831).




• Brugada algorithm also commonly utilized – see below.




• Known BBB: ventricular conduction delay (RBBB, LBBB, IVCD) with similar morphology and axis as seen on prior / baseline ECG




• Evidence of His conduction: QRS has sharp initial deflection (suggests initial use of His- Purkinje system followed by aberrancy)




• Pre-excitation on baseline ECG → supports antidromic AVRT or pre-excited atrial fibrillation




• R wave peak time < 40msec (measured in lead II and aVR)





Other important considerations:




• Hyperkalemia, antiarrhythmic drugs (digoxin, class IA or IC, amiodarone), TCA overdose




• Pacemaker-mediated/endless loop tachycardia: retrograde VA conduction of V-paced beat misidentified as native A-beat → V- pacing. ECG shows V pacing at upper rate limit




• Sensor induced tachycardia: inappropriate sensing of nonphysiologic stimuli (vibrations, electrocautery, etc.) and pacing.























MANAGEMENT OF VT (also see ACLS: Tachycardia)
• Often no way to confidently distinguish VT vs SVT with aberrancy. If there is any doubt, treat like VT




• Consider underlying processes: active ischemia, CAD with scar, electrolyte derangement (low K, low Mg), drug toxicity, indwelling lines, thyrotoxicosis




• Check and replenish electrolytes (K>4, Mg>2)




• Review baseline ECG for evidence of long QT or pre-excitation

Symptomatic or very high burden: nodal blockade AADs (amio, procainamide) Can be prompted by PVC (BB>CCB), then AADs Baseline prolonged QTc: magnesium 2-4g falling on T wave of previous




Stable and sustained (>30 seconds): antiarrhythmic over 10-15min, ↑HR (isoproterenol, overdrive beat (R on T phenomenon) agent (e.g. amiodarone, lidocaine, procainamide [WPW]) pacing), ↓QTc (lido), avoid bradycardia (no Note: isoproterenol = pure Unstable → synchronized cardioversion (100J) if pulse; amio, CCB/BB) chronotrope will reduce RoT defibrillation if pulseless




VT Storm: ≥3 sustained episodes of unstable VT within 24 hours




• Call EP +/- MCS Shock Team




• Lido bolus (preferred if prolonged QTc), Amio bolus (careful if long QT), consider co-admin propranolol 40mg q6 (esp. if s/p multiple defibrillations) [JACC2018;71:1897]




• Anti-tachycardia pacing (ATP): overdrive pacing at a faster rate than VT




• Treat / minimize ischemia: urgent revascularization, IABP to improve coronary perfusion, reduce preload / afterload




• Reduce autonomic tone: intubation and sedation, stellate ganglion block/cardiac sympathetic denervation




• Catheter ablation: In refractory cases, some evidence for ablation first strategy in ischemic CM (VANISH trial, VANISH2 trial)

ATRIAL FIBRILLATION


Epidemiology (LancetEuro2024;37:100786))




• RF: age, obesity, HTN, smoking, EtOH, DM, previous MI, HF, OSA




• Recurs in majority of cases due to secondary precipitant (surgery, infection, MI, thyrotoxicosis, acute alcohol, PE)




• Higher incidence in Caucasian and male patients (JACC 2020;76:2982)




• Racial, ethnic, and gender inqeuities persist in AF screening and management (Circ 2024; 149: e1-e156)




Clinical Evaluation of New-Onset AF




• H&P: presence & timing of sx, HTN, DM, valve dz, HF, angina, congenital heart disease, OSA, FH of AF, acute precipitants (e.g.







New AF Classification (Circ2024;149:e1-e156)




Stage I: At-risk for AF




Presence of modifiable and non- modifiable RFs




Stage II: Pre-AF




Structural or electrical findings that predispose to AF (atrial enlargement or ectopy etc.)




Stage III: AF Spectrum




Spectrum including paroxysmal (3A, <7d), persistent (3B, >7d), long- standing persistent (3C, >12mo), or s/p successful AF ablation (3D)




Stage IV: Permanent AF




Decision is made to no longer pursue rhythm control

• ECG: absence of discernible p waves, irregularly irregular R-R intervals (if regularized, may represent escape rhythm and CHB)

• Labs: TFTs, LFTs, BUN/Cr, CBC, NT-proBNP, BMP (K,Mg)




• May also need longer term rhythm monitoring (Holter, Zio patch). Consider stress test if signs/sx of ischemic heart disease.

start with 150J (Biphasic)




If pressors needed: phenylephrine is first-line given reflex bradycardia




Higher HRs (>140) more likely to cause HoTN alone; lower HRs may cause HoTN if systolic or diastolic dysfxn, or decreased preload (“loss of atrial kick”)








Cardioversion (ALWAYS consider high risk of embolic stroke if any-interruptions in AC for 3 weeks prior)




• Indications: Urgent: ischemia, end-organ hypoperfusion, symptomatic hypotension, severe pulmonary edema; Elective: new-onset AF or unacceptable symptoms from persistent AF




• Synchronized Electrical Cardioversion (DCCV): start with 150J (biphasic),↑energy if NSR not achieved. See ACLS: Cardioversion.




• Chemical Cardioversion: success rate significantly higher for acute (<7d) compared with longer duration AF




• Anticoagulation (applies to BOTH chemical and electrical)




◦ Pre-cardioversion: if definitive new onset <48h: may proceed without anticoagulation. If Afib onset >48h or unclear: anticoagulate for 3w prior to cardioversion or obtain TEE/CT Pulmonary Vein immediately prior to cardioversion




◦ Post-cardioversion: anticoagulate for at least 4 weeks after cardioversion (risk of myocardial stunning and AF recurrence, but unproven efficacy). Anticoagulation beyond 4 weeks after reversion to NSR is based on CHA2DS2-VASc and HAS-BLED scores




Risk Assessment (Risk scores DON’T account for the complete spectrum of RFs - Individualize AF management)




• CHA2DS2-VASc: 1pt for CHF, HTN, Age 65-74, DM, female Sex, Vascular disease; 2pt for Age≥75, Stroke/TIA. CHA2DS2-VASc > CHADS2 in “truly low risk” subjects (ThrombHaemostasis2012;107:1172)




◦ Score 0 = no AC; Score 1 (2 in women)= no AC vs AC based on clinical judgment, generally lean towards AC initiation; Score ≥2 (≥3 in women) = AC




◦ NOT used to guide decision making for HOCM or mitral stenosis (MS) with moderate severity or greater.




Source content
• HAS-BLED: risk stratification of bleeding risk w/ oral AC. HTN (SBP>160); abnl renal function (CrCl<50); liver disease (cirrhosis or Bili 2x ULN or AST/ALT/AlkPhos 3x ULN); stroke; bleeding history; labile INR (<60% in Rx range); elderly (>65y); antiplatelet meds (ASA, NSAID); alcohol (>8 drinks/w) or other drug use. Score ≥3 suggests caution and regular follow-up




• SPARCtool can aid in risk/benefit assessment and choice of anticoagulation




Anticoagulation (AHA/ACC/HRS: Circ2024;149:e1-e156;Stroke2010;41:2731)




• Consider AF burden when estimating stroke risk (JAMA Card 2018;601). Subclinical AF is also associated w/ increased stroke/systemic embolism(NEJM2012;366:120). In these pts, AC reduces the risk of ischemic stroke but increases the risk of major bleeding, thus AC decision should be individualized




• DOACs vs warfarin: DOACs (dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban) recommended > warfarin in all except valvular AF, mod- severe mitral stenosis, HOCM, or mechanical valve. Warfarin may be > rivaroxaban in rheumatic heart dz (NEJM 2022;387:978).




DOACs: ↓risk of stroke, mortality, & ICH, ↑risk of GIB (Lancet2014;383:955), apixaban lowest GIB risk (Ann Intern Med 2022;175:1515)




• Dosing: see Anticoagulation Agents for dosing. Dose-reduce apixaban to 2.5mg BID if 2/3: Cr ≥1.5, Wt ≤60kg, age ≥80




• Renal impairment: for pts w/ CrCl<15 or on dialysis, can use either warfarin or apixaban




• Bridging AC: see Anticoagulation Management




Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion (LAAO) - LAA is the source of at least 90% of thrombi in pts with CVA and AF




• Watchman device: in non-valvular AF, device placement → comparable stroke prevention to warfarin with ↓bleeding risk & improved mortality (JACC2017;70:2964). Consider if contraindication to long-term AC. .




• Surgical occlusion: decreases risk of stroke and systemic embolism. Grade 1A recommendation for pts with CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2 undergoing cardiac surgery in addition to continued AC (Circ2024;149:e1-e156).




Long-Term Rate vs Rhythm Control




• Traditionally, rate control considered noninferior to rhythm control for AF sx, CV mortality, & stroke risk (AFFIRM, RACE, PIAF, STAF, HOTCAFÉ, AF-CHF). Latest guidelines shifted with benefit of early rhythm control and reducing AF burden. (Circ2024;149:e1-e156)




• Rhythm control (antiarrhythmics and AF ablation) superior to usual care (rate control) for patients with recently diagnosed AF (within 1 year) and concomitant CV conditions in decreasing CV mortality, stroke, and hospitalization for HF or ACS (EAST-AFNET4)




◦ Consider rhythm control if persistent AF sx impairing quality of life, age <65, or comorbid HF (esp if systolic dysfxn)




◦ Restoration of NSR may lead to increased quality of life & exercise performance (NEJM2005;352:1861; JACC2004;43:241)




• Rate Control




◦ BB > CCB in achieving rate control (70% vs 54%), either alone or in combination with digoxin




◦ Digoxin alone is moderately effective in controlling V-rate at rest (time to onset 3-6 hrs), ineffective w/ high adrenergic tone




▪ Importantly: long-term digoxin a/w increased mortality in AF patients (JACC2018;71:1063)




◦ Targets: lenient rate control (resting HR <110) non-inferior to strict (HR <80) w/ similar outcomes in CV death, stroke, bleeding, arrhythmia, & hospitalization for HF (RACEII). Strict HR (or rhythm) control may be beneficial in younger pts or pts w/ HF




◦ Contraindications/Warnings: no nodal blockade if any evidence of pre-excitation on ECG (in these patients, IV procainamide is 1st line), cautious use in high-degree AVB. CCB should not be used in pts with LVEF <40% given negative inotropy




• Rhythm Control (Circ2012;125:381)




◦ Choice of Agents:




▪ No structural heart disease: flecainide,propafenone, dofetilide, dronedarone, sotalol, amiodarone




▪ Structural heart disease: CAD: dofetilide, dronedarone, sotalol, amiodarone; HF or LVH: amio, dofetilide




◦ “Pill-in-Pocket”: for patients with recent pAF and infrequent and well-tolerated episodes, ppx may have risk>benefit. PRN flecainide or propafenone + BB or CCB instead at symptom onset is safe and effective (NEJM2004;351:2384)




◦ Catheter ablation (pulmonary vein isolation [PVI]): Growing evidence behind PVI as safe & effective initial rhythm control strategy (NEJM 2021;384:305)↓long-term AF recurrence rate vs AADs in both pAF (MANTRA-PAF) & persistent AF (EHJ 2014;35:501). Ablation in pts w/ HF ↓morbidity/mortality (CASTLE-AF) and improves psychological distress. (JAMA 2023;330:925)




◦ AV nodal ablation with PPM: indicated when pharmacologic rate/rhythm control not achievable(JACC2014;64:2246)




ATRIAL FLUTTER (AFL, less prevalent but often coexists with or precedes AF)
• ECG: “sawtooth” P waves (F waves), atrial rate typically 250-300bpm w/ 2:1 conduction (~V-rate 150), though can be variable block, 3:1, or 4:1. 1:1 conduction can briefly precede VT/VF




◦ Type 1 (typical): reentrant loop in RA via cavo-tricuspid isthmus






▪ Counterclockwise: more common, inverted flutter waves II, III, aVF + upright flutter waves V1




▪ Clockwise: less common, upright flutter waves in II, III, aVF + inverted flutter waves in V1




◦ Type 2 (atypical): does not meet criteria for Type 1; is often faster and refractory to ablation

• Rate control: similar strategies (BB, CCB) to AF, but more difficult to successfully rate-control vs. AF




• Rhythm control: Ablation > AAD. Cavo-tricuspid isthmus (CTI) ablation for typical flutter >90% effective at 1y (CircArrhythmiaEP2009;2:393). However, prophylactic CTI ablation during PVI for AF pts without known AFL does not reduce incidence of AFL or recurrence of AF (Arryth EP Rev 2022; e10).

topics.text:
DEFINITION (Circ 2009; 119: e241)


• QT interval correlates with repolarization time of ventricles




• Normal: ≤460ms; Borderline (adult): 460-479ms (female), 450-459ms (male)




• Measure from beginning of QRS to end of T wave in a lead with T wave > 2mm (best in II, V5), define end point using tangent from peak of steepest slope to isoelectric line; can use ECG or caliper function on telemetry




• QTc is QT corrected for HR; linear (i.e., Hodges/Framingham) formulas are recommended by AHA (J Electrocardiology 2004;37:81)




• Can be calculated using MDCalc: Framingham and Fridericia provide best rate correction and mortality prediction (JAHA 2016;5:e003264)











ASSESSMENT OF QTC WITH UNDERLYING WIDE QRS (Heart Rhythm 2014;11:2273)
• Wide QRS (BBB/V-paced) lengthens QT interval; calculate using Mayo calculator, or with rough estimate using QT - (0.5*QRS). Must still account for HR (HeartRhythm.2014Dec;11(12)).




CONGENITAL LONG-QT SYNDROMES
• Majority of pts are asymptomatic, often discovered on ECG or QTc prolonged more than should be expected by drugs




• Sx: presyncope/syncope, hemodynamic compromise, sudden cardiac death; triggered by exercise, stress




• Tx: beta blocker for all, ICD if previous cardiac arrest and expected survival >1y (Class 1A Recommendation) (Circ2006;114:e385)




◦ BB thought to reduce early after-depolarizations and transmural dispersion of repolarizations, which can trigger arrhythmias




DRUG-INDUCED PROLONGED QT INTERVAL (Heart 2003;89:1363; NEJM 2004;350:1013)
• Drugs inhibit rapid K+ current causing prolonged ventricular repolarization & exaggerate heterogeneity in repolarization times in different layers of myocardium leading to reentry and tachyarrhythmia




Danger of prolonged QT = increased risk of Torsades de Pointes (TdP), which can degenerate into VF




Longer QT increases risk for “R on T” phenomenon and development of TdP (higher risk if PVCs)









Risk factors for TdP in Hospitalized Pts




(Circ2010;121:1047)




Demographics




Elderly, female, congenital long QT syndrome, anorexia/starvation, hypothermia




Comorbidities




Renal failure, hepatic dysfunction, drug-drug interactions, HF, MI, LVH, hypothyroidism, stress cardiomyopathy




Rhythm-related




QTc >500ms, bradycardia (sinus, AV block, ectopy causing pauses), PVCs




Electrolytes




Hypomagnesemia,




hypokalemia, hypocalcemia




Medication-




related




QT-prolonging drugs (esp. IV infusions, >1 concurrently), diuretic use, beta blocker use








Class of Drug




QT-Prolonging Drugs [common, high-risk, (low-risk)]: (BrJClinPharm2010;70:16;Circ2020:142:e214)




Antiarrhythmics




CLASS IA/C: quinidine, disopyramide, procainamide, flecainide, propafenone




CLASS III: sotalol, dofetilide, ibutilide, dronedarone, amiodarone - oralamiodarone rarely associated w/ TdP due to uniform delay in repolarization across myocardium




Antimicrobials




ANTIBIOTIC: azithromycin, erythromycin, clarithromycin,




levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, (ciprofloxacin),




(metronidazole)




ANTIFUNGAL: fluconazole, voriconazole, (ketoconazole)




ANTI-MALARIAL: quinine, quinidine, chloroquine, (also hydroxychloroquine)




Antipsychotics




haloperidol IV, thioridazine, chlorpromazine, ziprasidone,




quetiapine, risperidone, olanzapine, haloperidol oral, clozapine




Antidepressants




Clomipramine, imipramine, citalopram, escitalopram,




(fluoxetine), (sertraline), (trazodone), (mirtazapine)




Anti-emetics




ondansetron IV>oral, droperidol, (metoclopramide)




Others




Methadone, propofol, hydroxyzine, (loperamide),




(albuterol), (donepezil)







MONITORING FOR QT/QTC PROLONGATION
• Check QTc before and 12h after initiation/increased dose of QT-prolonging drug. Continue monitoring if prolongation is seen.




◦ Check QTc 2h post loading-dose of sotalol or dofetilide








• Class I indications for QTc monitoring with ECG (Circ2004;110:2721)




◦ Initiation of QT-prolonging medication and dose changes q8-12h




◦ Overdose of proarrhythmic drug




◦ New bradyarrhythmia




◦ Severe hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia




2:12













MANAGEMENT OF ACQUIRED LONG QT
• Stop offending drug if QTc >500ms or increase in QTc of >60ms




• ECG should be checked for bradyarrhythmias & signs of impending TdP (RonT, above). Stop drugs causing bradycardia.




• Check electrolytes & replenish to supratherapeutic levels (K: 4.5-5, Mg: 2-2.5)




• If patient develops TdP: See ACLS: Wide complex tachycardia page

2. High risk (“early invasive,” within 24h): temporal change in troponin, ECG changes (transient STE, STD, TWI), high risk pt (GRACE>140)




a. Conflicting results between TIMAC (NEJM2009;360:2165) and VERDICT (Circ2018;138:2741) trials about outcome benefit of early cath. However, both show improved outcomes with early cath in patients with GRACE >140




3. Intermediate risk (“delayed invasive,” within 72h): none of above but risk factors at baseline (e.g. EF <40%, GFR <60)




4. Low risk (“ischemia guided,” no cath): no risk factors, GRACE <109, TIMI 0-1 OR not good candidate for angiography

Source content
PCI vs CABG: Selection of revascularization strategy should be based on the acuity of the patient’s condition, the angiographic characteristics of the culprit lesion, and the complexity of the patient’s anatomy and, when appropriate, should include a Heart Team




discussion (Guideline: Circulation 2022;145:4). CABG often preferred for 3VD (NEJM2009;360:961), L main disease (NEJM2016;375:2223), 2VD with prox LAD stenosis or EF <50%, DM + 2VD w/ involvement of LAD (NEJM2012;367:2375).




Multivessel Disease PCI Strategies




◦ STEMI w/o cardiogenic shock: complete revascularization strategy (culprit + non-culprit) has ↓risk of CV death and MI at 3y (COMPLETE, NEJM2019;381:1411)




◦ STEMI OR NSTE-ACS + cardiogenic shock: culprit-lesion only PCI has a ↓risk of death/RRT (CULPRIT-SHOCK, NEJM 2018;379:1699). Consider staged complete revascularization




◦ NSTE-ACS w/o cardiogenic shock: complete revascularization strategy (BIOVASC, Lancet 2023;401:1172)




ADJUNCTS TO REVASCULARIZATION
Adjuncts at Presentation:




1. ASA: established mortality benefit, give to all pts in an immediate load/maintenance strategy (325mg/81mg) (Lancet1988;2:8607)




2. Peri-Intervention Anticoagulation: start on Dx of ACS. Usually stopped after PCI if no additional indication for AC (eg Afib, PE). If no PCI and medically managed, usually d/c at 48h if ECG changes improving and c/f ongoing ischemia resolved (BMJ1996;313:652). If chronically on warfarin/DOAC, discuss transition to short acting AC with pharmacy pre-cath.




◦ UFH: Standard. Start gtt w/ bolus and use low intensity PTT goal (50-70). Anti-Xa protocol also available. No bolus if giving lytics or if on warfarin and INR<2




◦ LMWH: possible reduction in death w/ minimal evidence for ↑major bleeding, trials vs UFH largely null (BMJ2012;344:e553)




◦ Fondaparinux: preferred to UFH/LMWH if medically managed. Contraindicated in PCI ↑catheter thrombosis/complications (JAMA2006;295:1519)




◦ GPIIb/IIa Inhibitors: eptifibatide (Integrilin) . Initiated in cath lab if PCI high-risk (extensive thrombus)




◦ Bivalirudin/Argatroban: direct thrombin inhibitor, preferred for patients w/ HIT. Emerging evidence suggests benefit over UFH in STEMI (BRIGHT-4 Lancet 2022;400:1847)




3. Statin: atorvastatin 80mg daily regardless of baseline LDL (NEJM2004;350:1495)




◦ Early high-dose statin within 24-96h may reduce death/adverse cardiac events if given pre-PCI (JACC2009;54:2157; JAMA 2018;319:1331). Early anti-inflammatory effect may stabilize plaque (JAMA2001;285:1711; JAMA2004;291:1071)




◦ If very high risk clinical ASCVD w/ LDL-c >70 mg/dL, add ezetimibe and consider PCSK9i (JACC2019;73:3168)




4. Nitrates: TNG SL (0.3-0.6mg) x3, if refractory → gtt (start 5-10mcg/min titrate to chest pain free). Nitropaste and gtt have shorter half-life than SL if c/f HoTN. No mortality benefit. Caution in inferior MI/RVMI, SBP<100, or PDEi use in last 48h. If refractory CP indication for earlier cath.




5. Morphine: not recommended. Consider only if unacceptable level of pain refractory to TNG, careful if suspicious for inferior MI/RVMI




6. Discontinue NSAIDs: ↑risk of mortality, re-infarction, HF, and myocardial rupture after ACS




Adjuncts to start within 24h or Post-Revasc




7. P2Y12 Inhibitors: . Controversial benefit & may delay CABG by 5- 7d (Circulation 2022;145:4). )




◦ Ticagrelor: ↓mortality compared to clopidogrel w/o increasing major bleeding. Reversible with platelet transfusion. Side effect: dyspnea (14-21%, often mild & transient, but can be severe enough to warrant discontinuation), risk of pneumonitis w/ alveolar hemorrhage. Avoid in liver disease, prior CVA, oral AC (PLATO, NEJM2009;361:1045).




◦ Prasugrel: ↓death, MI, CVA compared to ticag (NEJM2019;381:1524). Contraindicated if prior TIA/CVA, wt <60kg, or >75y




◦ Clopidogrel: ↓death, repeat MI when load/maintenance with PCI (Lancet2001;358:527I). Prodrug, metabolized by CYP219, less effective in those with LOF allele (NEJM2009;360:354). May benefit from PPI ppx for ↓UGIB (NEJM2010;363:1909). ↓Bleeding compared to ticagrelor and prasugrel but ↑ischemic events (Circulation 2020;142:150).




◦ Cangrelor: IV reversible inhibitor with immediate onset and return of platelet function in 1h.




DAPT duration: Default 12 months after ACS. Use DAPTscore to help risk stratify. Evolving movement to shorten DAPT duration (Select DAPT trials: TWILIGHT, TICO, STOPDAPT-2, SMART CHOICE, GLOBAL LEADERS, MASTER DAPT, HOST-EXAM)




Bottom line: In select patients, single agent P2Y12 inhibitor after 1-3 months (vs. longer duration DAPT) is non-inferior in reduction of cardiovascular events, with reduced bleeding. Decisions on DAPT should involve interventional cardiology




◦ If on longterm AC (eg AFib, PE): P2Y12 inhibitor + DOAC > triple therapy. ↓bleeding and non-inferior for ischemic events (AUGUSTUS NEJM2019;380;1509; RE-DUAL PCI NEJM2017;377:1513; NEJM2016;375:2423). (Guideline JACC 2021;77:629).




▪ Common example: initiate triple therapy (ASA/clopidogrel/AC) for 1-4wks and then d/c ASA → AC + clopidogrel




8. Beta Blockers: start within 24h (1B for STEMI, 1A for NSTE-ACS), mortality benefit. Consider early initiation if ischemic arrhythmias present. Not indicated for stable ischemic heart disease s/p cath, but rec’d after CABG (Circulation 2022;145:4). Long term BB s/p MI w/ LVEF >50%, does not reduce mortality or recurrent MI (NEJM 2024;390:1372)




◦ Caution in decompensated HF, ↑risk for cardiogenic shock (>70y, SBP <120, HR >110 or <60)




◦ Contraindications: shock, cocaine-induced MI, PR>240ms, 2nd or 3rd degree AVB, severe bronchospasm (Lancet2005;366:1622)




9. ACEi or ARB: start ACE within 24h in all patients if BP/renal function normal; mortality benefit in anterior STEMI; use ARB if intolerant of ACE. ARB > ACE in patients with HF or LVEF <40% (Circulation 2008; 117:269).




10. Aldosterone antagonist: s/p MI on ACE and BB, and have LVEF<=40 + DM or sx of HF (Circulation 2008; 117:269)




11. Lifestyle: smoking cessation, BP <130/80 (esp. if comorbid DM or CKD), cardiac rehab, depression screening; Flu vaccination




Emily Manning

• Note: RAO caudal: best overall view & best for LCx; LAO caudal: LM, prox LAD, prox LCx; LAO + RAO cran: mid+distal LAD




LEFT VS RIGHT HEART CATHETERIZATION
• LHC: Arterial access (radial, fem). Assess coronary anatomy/lesions (described as coronary angiogram), LV & Ao pressures; PCI




• RHC: Venous access (IJ, fem). Assess hemodynamics (see Pulmonary Artery Catherization); cardiac biopsies (usually RV)




CORONARY ANATOMY
• LCA and RCA & their branches create two rings around the heart: RCA + LCX in AV groove; LAD + PDA in IV groove




• 80% of PDA arises from RCA (right dominant), thus inferior MI more likely due to RCA lesion; 10% from LCx; 10% co-dominant




PREPARATION FOR CATHETERIZATION
• NPO MN vs clear liquid diet at midnight, then NPO 2hr prior (EHJ 2024:45:47) ; INR<2 for radial, <1.8 for fem/IJ; monitor Cr, no ppx abx. Cont ASA, statin, BB. Hold AC (ellucid): UFH gtt (hold when on call), LMWH (hold tx dose 24h prior, DVT ppx 12h prior), DOACs >48hr or >72hr if CrCl<30. Hold metformin (1d pre, 2d post), may hold ACEi or SGLT2i (procedure dependent)




• Document b/l radial, femoral, popliteal, DP pulses, & Allen’s test. Check for bruits. Note history of HIT, PAD, Ao aneurysm/dissection




• Contrast allergy: pre-tx w/ steroids & benadryl if patient has documented allergy.




• Respiratory distress: patient will need to lie flat; consider intubation if prohibitive hypoxemia/pulmonary edema




• Pre-hydration w/ crystalloids and NAC/bicarb have not been shown to prevent CIN in most patients with moderate CKD (Lancet 2017;389:1312; NEJM2018;378:603); CINriskcalculator




PERCUTANEOUS CORONARY INTERVENTION CONSIDERATIONS
• Access: fewer bleeding/vascular complications if radial (vs femoral) esp for PCI iso ACS, possible ↓death in ACS (JACC2018;71:1167); due to radial vasospasm, CCB and/or nitrogylcerin is administered along with UFH to prevent arterial occlusion




• Identifying HD significant lesions: fractional flow reserve (FFR), diastolic hyperemia-free ratio (DFR), and instant wave free ratio (iFR) assess functional impact of lesion; intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) evaluates lumen diameter, lesion length, and lesion calcification




• Contraindications to stents: predicted DAPT non-adherence, anticipated major surgery within treatment time, elevated bleeding risk




• Antiplatelet: 81mg ASA indefinitely (Circ2016;134:e123). P2Y12 inhibitor post cath. DAPT duration decided with interventional team




◦ Not high bleeding risk: ACS → 12mo DAPT; stable IHD → ≥6mo DAPT if DES or ≥1mo if BMS




◦ High bleeding risk: ACS → 6mo DAPT, consider DAPT 1-3mo followed by P2Y12i; stable IHD → ≥3mo DAPT if DES or ≥1mo if BMS, consider 1-3mo DAPT followed by P2Y12i (JACC Cardiovasc Interv 2024;17:2197)




◦ Triple therapy for patients requiring AC: see ACS. Usually, 1 wk triple therapy then P2Y12 inhibitor + DOAC




POST-PROCEDURE CARE
• Femoral access: 4-6h bedrest (HOB<30°) after procedure. Closure devices decrease time needed for bedrest




◦ Groin checks immediately, 6h, 8h post-procedure: check b/l pulses, palpate for pulsatile masses, auscultate for bruits




◦ Sheaths: usually removed when PTT<60, confirm with interventional fellow; only fellows remove sheaths




• Radial access: TR band for 4-6h driven by RN protocol. If paresthesias/numbness, examine, check finger sat probe for perfusion, can remove several mLs of air from band if necessary and if no complications. NOTE: if hematoma do not remove until fellow assesses




POST-CATHERIZATION COMPLICATIONS
• Access site complications: always inform the interventional fellow who performed the procedure, diagnose by exam and US




◦ Hematoma: mass w/o bruit. Apply compression. Fellow may recommend FemoStop device if unable to control




◦ Pseudoaneurysm: pulsatile mass with bruit at access site. Tx w/ compression; if <2cm, may require thrombin injection or surgery if >2 cm. Urgent arterial US & Vascular Surgery consult




◦ AV fistula: continuous bruit with no mass. Evaluate w/ arterial US. Surgical repair usually necessary




◦ Limb ischemia: from thrombus, dissection, or malpositioned closure device. Evaluate pulses, limb warmth, & PVR




◦ Retroperitoneal bleed: presents within hours post-cath, often with hemodynamic instability ± flank pain ± ecchymoses. STAT CT A/P if stable. Obtain large bore IV access, IVF, transfuse, discuss with attending about stopping/reversing anticoagulation




• Other complications:




◦ Infection: higher risk with vascular closure devices




◦ Atheroembolism: eosinophilia; livedo reticularis; blue toes; mesenteric ischemia; acute, subacute, or chronic renal dysfunction




◦ CIN: occurs within 24-72h with peak Cr 1-5d post contrast load; risk correlated with contrast load and initial GFR




◦ Tamponade: narrow PP, hypotension 2/2 coronary/cardiac perf. Check pulsus (>10 mmHg), STAT TTE, alert cath fellow.




◦ MI/CVA: due to in-stent thrombosis (MI) or distal embolization post-cath (CVA). Discuss all CP/neuro changes with cath fellow




◦ Radiation injury: more common in CTO cases; occurs days to weeks after PCI; ranges from erythema to skin ulceration




◦ Delayed Hemostasis: apply indirect pressure several cm cranial to site of skin access. Page gen cards fellow to discuss escalation to cath fellow/vasc surg (see ellucid escalation pathway)

topics.text:
BASICS
• Non-invasive cardiac testing includes functional and anatomic testing




• Approach to testing: 1) clinical question being asked, 2) symptom acuity, 3) baseline CVD risk/known CAD hx, 4) patient-specific C.I.




• For guideline-based assistance in decision making, use Stressing Wisely. For examples of (+) and (-) tests, use Radiopaedia.




ROLE OF NON-INVASIVE CARDIAC TESTING IN CHEST PAIN EVALUATION





Source: 2021 ACC/AHA Guidelines for Evaluation and Diagnosis of Chest Pain (Circ 2021;144:e368-e454)




Deciding between CCTA (anatomic) and stress imaging in an intermediate-high risk patient:




• CCTA favored: Age<65y and no prior CAD, rule out obstructive CAD, detect non-obstructive CAD, prior functional study w/o conclusive results, bypass graft assessment, known anomalous coronaries, parallel evaluation of aorta, pulmonary arteries, or LAA




• Stress imaging favored: Age>65y, if known >50% (obstructive) CAD to assess for specific areas of ischemia, prior CCTA w/o conclusive results, parallel evaluation for scar or microvascular dysfunction (PET or CMR)




• CCTA has higher sensitivity and similar angiography rates as conventional stress imaging; however, CCTA may lead to better outcomes overall as it can detect non-obstructive CAD and therefore drive preventive care (NEJM 2018;379:924)




STRESS/FUNCTIONAL TESTING
• Indications:




◦ Diagnose CAD: Workup stable angina in pts with intermediate-high risk of CAD. Consider spectrum of non-invasive tests vs. cath in intermediate-risk pts presenting with more acute sx. Not indicated in pts with no symptoms or at low risk




◦ Evaluate new or changing sx concerning for ischemia in pts with known CAD




◦ Post-revascularization: Evaluate pts with angina or asymptomatic pts if incomplete revasc or >2y post-PCI/5y post-CABG.




◦ Pre-op risk assessment: If indicated (see Perioperative Medicine)




◦ Other: Newly diagnosed HF or cardiomyopathy likely secondary to ischemia, functional capacity (for exercise prescription), viability testing, valvular disorders, dobutamine stress echo in LFLG AS, quantify microvascular disease (PET)




• Contraindications: Untreated ACS, MI within 2d, high risk or LM CAD, uncontrolled arrhythmia, ADHF, severe AS or HOCM, recent DVT/PE, acute myo-/peri-/endocarditis, aortic dissection, uncontrolled HTN




• Preparation: NPO 3h prior, longer if imaging or adenosine. Must reverse DNR/DNI for test




◦ If the question is “Does the patient have CAD?” → hold BB and nitrates




◦ If the question is “How well are meds working in known CAD?” → continue BB and nitrates




◦ Hold BB >24h for dobutamine stress test; hold caffeine >12h for adenosine




▪ Positive test results: Optimize medical rx. Decision re: angiography/revascularization varies by pt (degree of sx, tolerance of medical therapy). In ISCHEMIA trial, initial revasc vs. medical therapy did not reduce risk of ischemic CV events for pts with moderate to severe stable ischemic heart disease (NEJM2020;382:1395). In pts w/ stable angina, PCI does not increase exercise tolerance (Lancet 2018;391:31), but for pts who cannot tolerate medical therapy, PCI improved symptoms (NEJM 2023;389:2319)




• Caveats:




◦ Majority of vulnerable plaques are angiographically insignificant (<70% stenosis) → CCTA more sensitive for their detection




◦ Angiographically significant 3VD may produce false-negative vasodilator stress test → ”balanced ischemia”




▪ Balanced ischemia can be detected as transient ischemic dilatation (enlargement of LV cavity during stress)




▪ PET has higher accuracy in 3VD than SPECT/MIBI, because PET quantifies blood flow




.




Approach to choosing a stressor and evaluation modality:
Approach to choosing a stressor and evaluation modality:




• See Table 5 for full list of contraindications by test type (Circ 2021;144:e368-e454).




Choosing a stressor:




◦ Exercise: Preferred if patient can reach goal exertion. More relevant to real-world stress




◦ Adenosine/Regadenoson:




▪ Mechanism: Vasodilation via cAMP, detect ischemia by coronary steal (stenosed coronary arteries are unable to further dilate, creating a relative perfusion deficit in diseased vessels).




▪ Side effects: Wheezing, bradycardia, HoTN. Caution if ACTIVE bronchospasm, high grade AVB, SSS, severe AS




◦ Regadenoson (vs adenosine) has decreased respiratory/conduction side effects, is more cost-effective in obese pts, but caution if seizure hx (reversal agent aminophylline ↑seizure risk)




◦ Dobutamine:




▪ Mechanism: Positive inotropy and chronotropy via β-1 receptor agonism. Extremely high dose (up to 40 mcg/kg/min)




▪ Side effects: tachyarrhyth. Caution if MI <48h, hx malignant arrhyth, sev AS, HOCM, sev HTN, sev PAH, aortic dissection




Choosing an evaluation modality:




◦ ECG: Only used as stand-alone with exercise. Do not use with any longstanding ST/T wave abnormalities.




◦ TTE: Can define ischemia severity and risk-stratify. Additional info on hemodynamics/valves. ECG also obtained simultaneously.




▪ Do not use in pts with LBBB, V-pacing, or extensive wall motion abnormalities at rest




◦ Nuclear imaging (PET or SPECT/MIBI myocardial perfusion imaging):




▪ Uses a radiotracer (MIBI in SPECT, multiple options in PET) to detect areas of ↓perfusion between rest and stress states. Can measure LV function, transient LV dilatation, myocardial blood flow reserve. PET can detect microvascular ischemia.




▪ More expensive than TTE & high amount of radiation (SPECT > PET)




▪ PET more Sn & Sp than SPECT with faster image acquisition. Less widely available & more expensive. Additional uses for imaging in rheumatologic (i.e. cardiac sarcoid) and oncologic contexts (i.e. cardiac myxoma, metastases).




◦ Cardiac MRI (CMR):




▪ Localize ischemia and infarction, assess LV and RV function, determine myocardial viability. Can also detect microvascular dysfunction and tissue properties of the heart (inflammation, scarring, infiltration, cardiac tumors, pericardial disease)




Exercise Tolerance Test (ETT):




• Approach: ETT refers to exercise + ECG (cheap, available), or exercise + imaging eval (TTE, SPECT) (↑sensitivity)




• Protocols: Bruce (large changes in workload between stages), modified Bruce (for less fit pts → adds stages of lower workload)




• Assess: exercise duration, METs, BP/HR response, HR recovery, double product (HR x SBP), DukeTreadmillScore (estimates risk of CAD in pts w/ chest pain undergoing exercise stress testing (Circ1998;98:1622)).




• Diagnostic if: >85% max-predict HR (220-age), peak double product (HRxBP) >20k, HR recovery (HRpeak – HR1min post-exercise) >12, STEs - also localize to vascular territory




• Increased probability of ischemia with: ↑ # of leads with STD especially horizontal or downsloping, ↑ degree of max STD, ↓ METs when ECG changes occur, ventricular ectopy during recovery, increased time to recovery of ECG, failure of SBP to rise with exercise.




Viability testing:




• Indication: Determine viability of ischemic myocardium (assess for hibernating tissue) that may be salvaged w/ revascularization.




• Modalities: SPECT, PET, TTE, MRI with exercise or pharmacologic stress. Looking for metabolic or contractile reserve.




ANATOMIC TESTING
Coronary CTA (CCTA):




• Indications:




◦ Evaluate for the presence and extent of CAD. Primarily anatomic info, though offers plaque characterization and CT FFR.




◦ Asymptomatic pts: NOT for screening use. Low-risk pts with sx: high NPV (99%) for CAD rule-out (JACC2008;52:1724). Moderate-risk pts with sx: reasonable for risk stratification (especially after equivocal stress test).




• Preparation: Requires cardiac gating (goal HR 60-70, may need to give BB) and respiratory gating (breath hold for 5+ sec).




• Results:




◦ 2y ACS risk significantly elevated if high-risk plaque (16%) and/or stenotic disease (6%) (JACC2015;28:337)




◦ Higher Sn & Sp for coronary stenosis compared to cMRI (Annals2010;152:167)




• Caveats: Less useful in pts with extensive calcifications (older) or stented vessels due to “blooming” artifact (cannot eval patency).




Coronary Artery Calcium (CAC) Scan:




• Indications:




◦ Risk-assessment for ASCVD risk stratification. Used to guide decision-making for primary prevention/statin therapy in asymptomatic pts, ≥40y at intermediate-risk (7.5-19.9% 10y ASCVD risk). DO NOT use in symptomatic pts or high risk pts.




• Preparation: Non-gated, non-contrast (if done independent of CCTA) CT scan.




• Results: MESA score accounts for CAC score and is able to refine 10 year risk estimates




◦ If CAC score 0 and pt without significant risk factors, reasonable to defer statin therapy for up to 5 years (Circ2019;140:496).




◦ If CAC score ≥100 or >75%ile for age & gender, recommend aggressive lifestyle changes, ASCVD RF modification (BP, smoking cessation, diabetes treatment), & statin therapy (JACC2019;73:285)




Cardiac MRI: provides both stress/functional and anatomic testing options

topics.text:
BASIC FRAMEWORK


Diagnosis of heart failure vs cardiomyopathy (CM)




• Heart failure is a clinical diagnosis – requires signs/symptoms of volume overload (e.g. orthopnea, leg swelling, crackles, ↑JVP) attributable to a structural or functional impairment in ventricular ejection or filling




• Heart failure ≠ cardiomyopathy – a CM is an abnormality in myocardial structure or function, usually visualized by TTE (does not require signs/symptoms of volume overload)




Classifications of heart failure




• LVEF classes: HFpEF (LVEF >50%), HFmrEF (‘mildly reduced’ EF; LVEF 41-49%), HFrEF (LVEF ≤40%), HFimpEF (‘improved’ EF; previous LVEF ≤40% and a follow-up measurement of LFEF > 40%)




• ACC/AHA Stage and NYHA Functional Class (see Figure)











Identifying underlying etiology







Category




Cardiomyopathy etiologies




Most common




ischemic, hypertensive, valvular




Metabolic




diabetic, nutritional deficiency (e.g. beriberi)




High-output




septic, peripartum, hyperthyroid, anemia, liver failure, Paget’s, AV shunts




Toxins/drugs




alcohol, cocaine/amphetamines, chemotherapy, immune checkpoint inhibitors




Infectious




HIV, coxsackie, echovirus, EBV, CMV, Lyme, Chagas disease, tuberculosis




Infiltrative




amyloidosis (ATTR or AL), hemochromatosis, sarcoidosis, Löffler’s




Genetic




hypertrophic cardiomyopathy/HOCM, ARVC, familial neuromuscular disorders, glycogen storage disorders, LVNC




Inflammatory




connective tissue diseases, giant cell myocarditis




Other




pulmonary (cor pulmonale), stress-induced (Takotsubo), tachyarrhythmia-induced, pericardial disease (e.g. constrictive pericarditis, pericardial effusion), radiation, carcinoid, idiopathic





NOTE: CM can be additional defined as ‘dilated,’ ‘hypertrophic,’ and ‘restrictive’ based on morphology/structure seen on imaging




Workup




• Initial workup: signs/sxs of volume overload, troponin, NTproBNP, ECG, tele, CXR, TTE




• Ischemic CM workup: family hx, smoking hx, lipid panel, A1c, see Non-Invasive Testing and Cardiac Catherization




• Non-ischemic CM workup: family hx, med hx, substance use hx, tox screen, β-hCG, iron studies, SPEP/UPEP/FLC, TSH, HIV, ANA




• Extended workup (when applicable): chest CT, cardiac MRI, RHC, endomyocardial biopsy, PYP scan, viral serology panel, Lyme serologies, T. cruzi serologies, ACE level, thiamine/carnitine/selenium, genetic testing, antimyosin Ab




Management of heart failure




• Treat the underlying causes of (1) cardiomyopathy and (2) decompensation triggers




• Basic elements of treatment: diuresis, afterload reduction, consideration of device/advanced therapies




• Guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT):






◦ HFrEF/HFmrEF/HFimpEF = BB, ACEi/ARB/ARNi, MRA, SGLT2i




◦ HFpEF = MRA, SGLT2i





2022 ACC/AHA HF Guidelines:




Circ 2022;145:895









• Cardiomyopathy-specific interventions: ischemic = PCI, CABG; valvular = TAVR, MitraClip, other valve interventions; tachyarrhytmia-induced = ablation, PPM, CRT; ATTR amyloid = tafamadis ↓TTR deposition (NEJM 2018;379:1007), acoramadis, vutrisiran; sarcoid = prednisone, steroid-sparing IST




CONSIDERATIONS FOR SELECT CARDIOMYOPATHIES

Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM) (Circulation 2024;149 :e1239)




Characteristics: LV and/or RV hypertrophy ± LVOT dynamic obstruction (HOCM), diastolic dysfxn, ischemia, MR; risk of SCD




Exam: SEM at LLSB/apex that augments with Valsalva or on standing (due to ↓preload); S2 paradox split, S4




Dx: ECG (prominent voltages w/ depol abnormalities, large Q waves in inferior/lateral leads, LAD, negative T waves in V2-V4 (apical HCM), TTE (LVH >15mm, SAM of MV, outflow tract gradient +/- provocative test), cMRI (late gadolinium enhancement [LGE] = fibrosis) Clinical genetic testing (mutation in ~70%) helpful for family screening; not useful for dx or risk stratification




Tx: avoid volume depletion or high dose vasodilators (may worsen obstruction); phenylephrine is pressor of choice if no response to IVF bolus for HoTN (↑afterload, stents open LVOT). Activity restriction, meds (disopyramide, BB > verapamil). Cardiac myosin inhibitors (e.g. aficamten, mavacamten) if LVEF ≥ 55% (VALOR-HCM); septal ablation or surgical myectomy if medically refractory, ICD ifhigh risk




Risk factors for SCD/VT: prior VT/SCD/unexplained syncope; FHx of SCD in 1° relative; massive LVH (>30mm); NSVT on Holter; abnormal BP response to exercise; burden of LGE on cMRI; h/o suspected cardiac syncope; EF<50%







• Amyloidosis (AL, TTR): HF + amyloid findings (e.g. renal), low voltage ECG, thick LV/RV on TTE, LGE in subendocardium on cMRI




• Hemochromatosis: hereditary or secondary, ECG with SVT, dilated LV on TTE, iron overload on T2 protocol of cMRI




• Sarcoidosis: ECG with atypical infarct pattern or block, patchy enhancement of basal and LV walls on cMRI




ACUTE DECOMPENSATED HEART FAILURE MANAGEMENT – FLOOR/SDU
Identify hemodynamic profile and triage accordingly (JACC2019;74:1966)






• Warm vs Cold: consider AMS, lactate, cool extremities, narrow pulse press




• Dry vs Wet: presence vs absence of congestion




• Evaluate for pulmonary congestion on exam. Pulm edema may be absent on CXR due to lymphatic compensation (Chest2004;125:669)




• Majority of HFrEF and HFpEF pts will be warm and wet




• See ‘Right Ventricular Failure’ for special considerations for patients with primarily right-sided heart disease











History




• Identify decompensation triggers: Mnemonic FAILURE – F = forgot meds, A = arrhythmia/anemia/afterload, I = infection/ischemia, L = lifestyle (salty diet), U = upregulation of cardiac output (e.g. pregnancy, hyperthyroid), R = renal failure, E = embolism. Other triggers: progression of CM, inadequate diuretic dose, meds (NSAIDs, steroids, CCB, anthracyclines), toxins (EtOH), new/worsened valve




• HF history (prior CM dx, dry weight, last NTproBNP, last TTE/EF, prior ischemic w/u, outpt cardiologist), accurate PAML, social/fam hx




Admission considerations




• Admission orders: tele, 2g Na-restricted diet, daily standing weights, strict I/Os, DVT ppx, (SDU only) electrolyte replenishment scales




• SDU admission indications: EF <25%, NTproBNP ≥ 2,500, arrhythmia-induced HF. Black & Latinx pts w/ HF are less likely to be admitted to cardiology services, contributing to racial inequities in HF outcomes (Circ Heart Fail 2019;12:e006214)




• Avoid: CCB (esp. non-dihydropyridines), NSAIDs, flecainide




• Check NT-proBNP (& weight) on admission. ADHF unlikely if NT-proBNP <300 (NPV 98%), likely if >450 (>900 if age >50) (Am J Cardiol 2005;95;948). Difficult to interpret in CKD/dialysis. May be falsely low in obesity, HFpEF




• Screen for and treat iron deficiency in all HF pts independent of Hgb (JACCHF2019;7:36)




◦ Dx: ferritin <100 or ferritin <300 + TSat <20% (JACC2017;70:776)




◦ Tx: replete with IV iron (JACC2018;71:782) to ↓sx, ↑functional capacity, and possibly improve outcomes (NEJM 2023;389:975)




Early/acute management




• Diuresis: ↓CVP, PCWP to optimize Starling curve mechanics & relieve sx (NEJM2017;377:1964;JACC2020;75:1178)




◦ Initial tx: IV loop (furosemide, torsemide, bumetanide), start w/ 20-40mg IV furosemide if diuretic-naïve otherwise start w/ 2-2.5x home dose (IV/PO). No difference b/w continuous gtt vs bolus (NEJM2011;364:797).See Advanced Diuresis




◦ Refractory diuresis: add metolazone 2.5-5mg (or chlorothiazide 500mg IV) administered 30min before loop diuretic. May need RHC to clarify hemodynamics or inotropes to augment diuresis. Acetazolamide (500mg daily), as well as dapagliflozin (10mg daily), may also augment successful decongestion (NEJM 2022;387:1185; EHJ 2023;44:2966). Step-up pharmacologic therapy superior to RRT in the setting of cardiorenal syndrome (NEJM2012;367:2296)




◦ Worsening renal function: Common occurrence. Mild-mod “Cr bumps” likely benign, should not necessarily preclude further diuresis if pt still congested (Circ2018;137:2016)




◦ Endpoints: target resolution of signs/symptoms of congestion. Daily weights, hemoconcentration, lung and JVP POCUS are useful adjuncts to ensure diuresis to euvolemia. B-lines on lung US portend ↑risk of HF admissions/death (EHJ 2016;37:1244)




• If acute pulmonary edema, NIPPV may improve mortality and reduce need for intubation (Annals2010;152:590)




• Vasodilators: arterial/venous dilation can relieve symptoms by ↓afterload, ↓PCWP. Consider esp. in severe HTN, acute MR or AR




◦ Floor: isosorbide dinitrate, hydralazine, nitropaste, captopril; SDU/CCU: nitro gtt, nitroprusside gtt (caution if uncorrected CAD)




• Home GDMT continuation: if not in cardiogenic shock or new AKI, continue ACEi/ARB/ARNi and βB (at fractionated dose) during ADHF (but do not newly initiate βB) (EHJ 2009;30:2186). Hold SGLT2i as it may preclude procedure




Guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT)




• HFrEF, HFmrEF (+/- HFimpEF): prioritize initiation of low-dose quadruple GDMT prior to d/c




◦ Beta-blockers (BB): initiate BB (carvedilol, metoprolol succ., bisoprolol) (COPERNICUS; MERIT-HF).Caution if recent inotropes




◦ RAAS inhibitors: if renal fxn stable, initiate/titrate ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) (PARADIGM-HF;PIONEER-HF),secondlineACEi/ARB (CONSENSUS;CHARM). Switch to ARNI from ACEi/ARB if no C.I./cost concerns, 36h washout period for ACEi prior to ARNI




◦ MRA: initiate spironolactone or eplerenone if CrCl>30 (EMPHASIS-HF;RALES). Watch for rebound hyperK after de-escalation of diuretics (check K, Cr within 72h of discharge)




◦ SGLT2i: dapaglifozin and empagliflozin reduce mortality and HF admissions regardless of DM (DAPA-HF; EMPEROR-Reduced)




◦ Guidance for GDMT in advanced CKD: JACCHF2019;7:371




◦ GDMT dosing - AHA/ACC/HFSA 2022 Guidelines (Circ 2022;145:895)

• HFpEF: improve volume overload with diuretics, treat comorbidities (DM, HTN, AF), add GDMT




◦ SGLT2i found to ↓CV death/hospitalizations in pts with EF >40% (EMPEROR-Preserved, DELIVER)




◦ Consider spironolactone if normal renal fxn/K, ↓CV death/admits in N/S Am. sites in TOPCAT (Circ2015;131:34)




◦ No proven benefit to BB (EHJ2018;39:26), ACEi (PEP-CHF), ARNi (PARAGON-HF), ARB (CHARM-Preserved;I-PRESERVE)




◦ New options: finerenone (nonsteroidal MRA) (NEJM 2024;391:1475), semaglutide (GLP1ra) (NEJM 2023;389:2221)




• ICD indicated if: ischemic CM w/ EF ≤30 or ≤35% w/ NYHA II-III; CRT if: EF ≤35% & prolonged QRS ± LBBB & some w/ EF ≤50% (see Cardiac Devices: PPM/ICD & guidelines for specifics:JACC2013;61:e6;EHJ2016;37:2129)




Pre-discharge optimization
Pre-discharge optimization




• Document d/c weight and NTproBNP, appt in HF Transitions Clinic, referral to cardiac rehab




• Optimization of GDMT as above




• Diuretic plan: determine maintenance oral diuretic dose and provide specific instructions for taking additional rescue doses. Consider inpatient observation on maintenance dose and decide if needs K replacement.




CARDIOGENIC SHOCK – CCU
• Stages: A. “At risk” B. “Beginning”=HDUS pt w/o hypoperfusion (e.g. oliguria, ↑lactate, ↑ Cr.), C. “Classic”=signs of hypoperfusion (HoTN maybe absent), D. “Deteriorating”=no improvement to initial therapy, E. “Extremis” (JSCAI 2021:1:1)




• Evaluation: ECG, troponin to r/o acute MI. TTE to exclude tamponade/mechanical lesions/contraindications to MCS




• Monitoring: A-line, consider PA catheter for inotropes/pressors and MVO2 monitoring




Immediate Management:




• If c/f acute MI, activate cath lab for PCI (only intervention proven to improve outcomes in cardiogenic shock) (NEJM1999;341:625)




• ). Escalating inotropes/pressors a/w poor outcomes. Evidence for early initiation of MCS




• Stabilize MAP with norepinephrine PRN prior to obtaining PA catheter to guide tailored therapy




Tailored Therapy: uses invasive hemodynamic monitoring (i.e., PAC) to guide medical therapy. See Pulmonary Artery Catheterization.




• Goals: tissue perfusion (↑CO, MAP), decongestion (↓CVP, PCWP), ventricular unloading (minimize myocardial O2 demand)




◦ Preload: LVEDV ∝ LVEDP ≈ PCWP; goal PCWP 14-18, PAD 16-20, CVP 8-12 → diuresis, UF with RRT




◦ Afterload: wall stress ∝ MAP (Laplace’s law); SVR = (MAP - CVP)/CO; goal MAP >60, SVR <800-1200




▪ Vasodilators: captopril, hydralazine, nitroprusside, TNG, isosorbide dinitrate




▪ Vasopressors: ↑afterload, sometimes needed to ↑MAP in mixed shock or to counteract vasodilatory effect of inodilators




◦ Contractility: ∝ CO for given preload/afterload; goal CO>4, CI >2.0-2.2, MVO2 >65




▪ Dobutamine (inodilator): β1>β2 agonist (↑production of cAMP); initial dose 0.5-1 mcg/kg/min




• Watch for tachycardia, ↑ventricular response to AF, arrhythmias, ischemia, HoTN, tachyphylaxis in infusions >24-48h




▪ Milrinone (inodilator): PDE-3 inhibitor (↓breakdown of cAMP); initial dose 0.125 mcg/kg/min




• Watch for tachycardia, arrhythmias, ischemia, HoTN. Compared to dobutamine, milrinone has longer half-life, greater pulmonary vasodilatation, slightly less chronotropy




• Preferred in patients w/ RV failure. Renally cleared. Often choice for home inotrope for palliative therapy




▪ Epi (inopressor): use if severe HoTN often in combo with inodilators. Watch for arrhythmias, end-organ hypoperfusion




◦ Advanced: consideration of need for MCS or transplant to improve systemic perfusion; see Mechanical Circulatory Support

topics.title: Right Ventricular Failure

runs.t: : governed by systemic venous return, PA pressure, pericardial compliance, and native contractility of the RV free wall and interventricular septum (where RV and LV are “tethered”)

◦ The RV is coupled to the high-compliance, low-resistance pulm circulation → RV ejects blood at lower pressure compared to LV → RV is more afterload sensitive than LV. RV can adapt to changes in volume > pressure.

: RV & LV interdependent → failure of RV → failure of LV via: (1) decreased LV preload, as RV output = LV preload & (2) septal bowing into LV, causing diastolic impairment (“Diastolic Ventricular Interaction”)

◦ ↑RV afterload (e.g. PE, hypoxemia, acidemia), ↑RV preload (e.g. L→R shunt or TV disease), or ↓RV contractility (e.g. MI, myocarditis) all lead to increased RV wall stress & resultant ischemia -> “death spiral”
: gradual ↑RV afterload (e.g. from pulmonary hypertension / pulmonic stenosis / tricuspid regurgitation)
: ↑JVP, Kussmaul’s sign (↑JVP with inspiration), peripheral edema, RV heave, pulsatile liver, split S2, new TR murmur
: RAD, R:S amplitude >1 in V1, p-wave > 2.5mm in inferior leads (P pulmonale), S1Q3T3 (RV strain in PE), atrial arrhythmias
: NT-proBNP, troponin, also ↑Cr and LFTs secondary to venous congestion (LFTs may be normal in chronic RV failure)
: PA/lateral CXR; chest CT → RV/LV ratio >0.9 suggests RV strain

: measure RV size/fxn/pressure to elucidate etiology. Aortic root, LA, RV should be ~1:1:1 in size (PSL view). RV should be < LV in size (Apical 4Ch view). RVEF based on displacement of base towards apex, correlates with
= tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (normal ≥ 17 mm; reflects apex-to-base shortening).
calculated from TR jet, correlates w/ RHC but can vary within 10mmHg (esp w/ lung disease, PPV)
RHC w/ placement of PA line
: gold standard for measurement of ventricular filling pressures, CO, PA pressures
: normal = 0.5, ↑ is sign of RV dysfunction; PAPi: (PAs – PAd)/CVP <0.9 = RV failure, for pts w/ VAD < 1.85 = RV failure;
(e.g. pericardial disease, RVMI, PE, hypoxemia, infections)
: judicious IVF (0.5-1L) in absence of CVP elevation (goal CVP 10-14 in RVMI)
: IV diuresis to ↓RV pressures, ↓functional TR, and improve LV CO; consider CRRT if refractory to diuresis
as propagates RV death spiral (↓CPP); Goal MAP>65 & MAP>mPAP
no clinical data regarding pressor of choice, but often choose vasopressin or norepinephrine (vaso affects PVR less than norepi)
: remove factors that ↑pulm vasc tone (e.g. hypoxemia, acidemia). Consider pulm vasodilators if evidence of PAH (inhaled>oral to deliver vasodilators to ventilated vascular beds)
iNO, prostacyclin agonists (epoprostenol (Veletri), inhaled or IV)
, endothelin antagonists (e.g. bosentan, ambrisentan), nitric oxide enhancers (e.g. PDE-5 inhibitors: sildenafil, tadalafil)
: milrinone (↓RV afterload by pulm vasodilation but ↑HoTN risk); epinephrine (↑RV contractility, ↑MAP). In RVMI, important to revascularize urgently as inotropes can exacerbate ischemia.
: if refractory RVF, consider RV MCS and/or biventricular support (ProtekDuo, Impella RP, VA-ECMO)

panels.title: INTUBATION AND MECHANICAL VENTILATION (Curr Heart Fail Rep 2012;9:228)

runs.t: • RV preload is “extrathoracic” and afterload is “intrathoracic” → intubation/PPV ↑ PVR & RV afterload→↑ RV dilation→“death spiral”
• Mech vent/NIPPV in RV failure precipitate risk for
trial of HFNC for hypoxemic respiratory failure preferred prior to MV/NIPPV given minimal effect on RV afterload.

◦ Drugs commonly used in intubation (BZDs, propofol, muscle relaxants) → tendency towards vasodilation and negative inotropy → decreased venous return → decreased RV/LV preload → systemic hypoTN → propagates “death spiral”
rapid sequence intubation w/ hemodynamically stable induction agents
(ketamine/etomidate >> propofol for induction) & push dose epinephrine (5-20mcg) or phenylephrine if emergent intubation; have norepi in line
: prevent hypoxemia & hypercarbia (↑PVR), consider moderate TV (~8cc/kg), low PEEP (<8 cm H2O), and moderate plateau pressure goal (<30 mmHg) to help minimize RV afterload
: check R-sided ECG leads in pts with inferior STEMI (10-15% have RV involvement)
◦ 1mm STE in V4R → 88% Sn, 78% Sp in inferior STEMI; STE III>II suggests RCA > LCx and RVMI
◦ High-grade AV block seen in ~50% of pts with RVMI
: pts with RVMI may initially benefit from fluid bolus;

topics.text:
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY AND ETIOLOGIES (NEJM 2023;388:1111)


• Normal RV function: governed by systemic venous return, PA pressure, pericardial compliance, and native contractility of the RV free wall and interventricular septum (where RV and LV are “tethered”)




◦ The RV is coupled to the high-compliance, low-resistance pulm circulation → RV ejects blood at lower pressure compared to LV → RV is more afterload sensitive than LV. RV can adapt to changes in volume > pressure.




• Acute RV Failure: RV & LV interdependent → failure of RV → failure of LV via: (1) decreased LV preload, as RV output = LV preload & (2) septal bowing into LV, causing diastolic impairment (“Diastolic Ventricular Interaction”)




◦ ↑RV afterload (e.g. PE, hypoxemia, acidemia), ↑RV preload (e.g. L→R shunt or TV disease), or ↓RV contractility (e.g. MI, myocarditis) all lead to increased RV wall stress & resultant ischemia -> “death spiral”




• Chronic RV Failure: gradual ↑RV afterload (e.g. from pulmonary hypertension / pulmonic stenosis / tricuspid regurgitation)





















CLINICAL FEATURES AND WORKUP (Circ 2018;137:e578-e622)
• Exam: ↑JVP, Kussmaul’s sign (↑JVP with inspiration), peripheral edema, RV heave, pulsatile liver, split S2, new TR murmur




• EKG: RAD, R:S amplitude >1 in V1, p-wave > 2.5mm in inferior leads (P pulmonale), S1Q3T3 (RV strain in PE), atrial arrhythmias




• Labs: NT-proBNP, troponin, also ↑Cr and LFTs secondary to venous congestion (LFTs may be normal in chronic RV failure)




• Imaging: PA/lateral CXR; chest CT → RV/LV ratio >0.9 suggests RV strain




• Echo: measure RV size/fxn/pressure to elucidate etiology. Aortic root, LA, RV should be ~1:1:1 in size (PSL view). RV should be < LV in size (Apical 4Ch view). RVEF based on displacement of base towards apex, correlates with TAPSE = tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (normal ≥ 17 mm; reflects apex-to-base shortening). RVSP calculated from TR jet, correlates w/ RHC but can vary within 10mmHg (esp w/ lung disease, PPV)




• RHC w/ placement of PA line: gold standard for measurement of ventricular filling pressures, CO, PA pressures




◦ Assessments of RV function – CVP/PCWP ratio: normal = 0.5, ↑ is sign of RV dysfunction; PAPi: (PAs – PAd)/CVP <0.9 = RV failure, for pts w/ VAD < 1.85 = RV failure; RV stroke work index: (mPAP – CVP) x (CI/HR) x 0.0136 (normal 8-12 g/m/beat/m2)




MANAGEMENT (Circ 2018;137:e578)
• Treat reversible causes (e.g. pericardial disease, RVMI, PE, hypoxemia, infections)




• Preload (CVP goal 8-12mmHg): both hypo- and hypervolemia can ↓CO




◦ Volume responsive (PE, RVMI): judicious IVF (0.5-1L) in absence of CVP elevation (goal CVP 10-14 in RVMI)




◦ Volume overload: IV diuresis to ↓RV pressures, ↓functional TR, and improve LV CO; consider CRRT if refractory to diuresis




• Afterload:




◦ Systemic: if pt hypotensive, start pressors – do not tolerate HoTN as propagates RV death spiral (↓CPP); Goal MAP>65 & MAP>mPAP (EHJ Acute CV Care 2022;11:77) no clinical data regarding pressor of choice, but often choose vasopressin or norepinephrine (vaso affects PVR less than norepi) (Crit Care Med 2007;35:2037)




◦ Pulmonary: remove factors that ↑pulm vasc tone (e.g. hypoxemia, acidemia). Consider pulm vasodilators if evidence of PAH (inhaled>oral to deliver vasodilators to ventilated vascular beds)




▪ Types: iNO, prostacyclin agonists (epoprostenol (Veletri), inhaled or IV), endothelin antagonists (e.g. bosentan, ambrisentan), nitric oxide enhancers (e.g. PDE-5 inhibitors: sildenafil, tadalafil)




• Contractility: milrinone (↓RV afterload by pulm vasodilation but ↑HoTN risk); epinephrine (↑RV contractility, ↑MAP). In RVMI, important to revascularize urgently as inotropes can exacerbate ischemia.




• Devices: if refractory RVF, consider RV MCS and/or biventricular support (ProtekDuo, Impella RP, VA-ECMO)




INTUBATION AND MECHANICAL VENTILATION (Curr Heart Fail Rep 2012;9:228)
• RV preload is “extrathoracic” and afterload is “intrathoracic” → intubation/PPV ↑ PVR & RV afterload→↑ RV dilation→“death spiral”




• Mech vent/NIPPV in RV failure precipitate risk for hemodynamic collapse & cardiac arrest; trial of HFNC for hypoxemic respiratory failure preferred prior to MV/NIPPV given minimal effect on RV afterload.




◦ Drugs commonly used in intubation (BZDs, propofol, muscle relaxants) → tendency towards vasodilation and negative inotropy → decreased venous return → decreased RV/LV preload → systemic hypoTN → propagates “death spiral”




◦ Consider rapid sequence intubation w/ hemodynamically stable induction agents (ketamine/etomidate >> propofol for induction) & push dose epinephrine (5-20mcg) or phenylephrine if emergent intubation; have norepi in line anticipating hypotension.




• Vent management: prevent hypoxemia & hypercarbia (↑PVR), consider moderate TV (~8cc/kg), low PEEP (<8 cm H2O), and moderate plateau pressure goal (<30 mmHg) to help minimize RV afterload




RIGHT VENTRICULAR MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION (ACC/AHA: Circ 2013;127:e362)
• EKG: check R-sided ECG leads in pts with inferior STEMI (10-15% have RV involvement)




◦ 1mm STE in V4R → 88% Sn, 78% Sp in inferior STEMI; STE III>II suggests RCA > LCx and RVMI




◦ High-grade AV block seen in ~50% of pts with RVMI




• Management: pts with RVMI may initially benefit from fluid bolus; caution w/ TNG (↓preload) & BB
